title: LGL Ltd. v. R (2000 FCA) Federal Court of Appeal Case
subject: Federal Court of Appeal decision on whether contract research performed for a third party qualified as SR&ED for the performer.
outcome: Appeal dismissed; FCA confirmed that expenditures reimbursed or funded by a client under contract reduced eligible SR&ED credits.
keyPhrase: LGL Ltd v The Queen 2000 FCA
summary: LGL Ltd. v. R. (2000 FCA) is the Federal Court of Appeal ruling that SR&ED territorial eligibility in Canada is assessed expenditure by expenditure, not project by project. For Canadian taxpayers, field work physically carried on outside Canada, and its allocable overhead, falls under subsection 37(2) of the Income Tax Act and cannot generate Investment Tax Credits.
metaDescription: Read the 2000 Federal Court of Appeal decision in LGL Ltd. v. R (The Queen) concerning Canadian SR&ED overhead and tax expenses.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in LGL Ltd. v. R. (rendered February 7, 2000, Docket A-139-99; reported at 2000 D.T.C. 6108 (FCA), 2000 CanLII 14931 (FCA)), affirming the judgment of Judge Donald G.H. Bowman at the Tax Court of Canada (rendered January 12, 1999, Docket 96-4726(IT)G; reported at [1999] 2 C.T.C. 2482, 99 D.T.C. 675 (TCC)), stands as the foundational appellate authority governing the territorial eligibility of Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) expenditures in Canada. The ruling resolved a critical doctrinal split within the Tax Court of Canada regarding whether an SR&ED project designed, directed, and analyzed in Canada can be treated as an "indivisible whole" when essential data collection or support activities must physically occur outside Canadian borders. By rejecting the holistic project-location theory and establishing a strict, two-stage analytical framework that separates project-level technical qualification from expenditure-by-expenditure geographic eligibility, the Federal Court of Appeal drew a bright-line boundary between domestic SR&ED expenditures eligible for refundable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Income Tax Act (Canada) (the "Act") and foreign research expenditures relegated to subsection 37(2).
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Claim

The appellant, LGL Limited ("LGL"), was a Canadian-incorporated environmental research and consulting enterprise owned and managed by Canadians, with primary operations based in Ontario. LGL specialized in conducting scientific investigations for government agencies, industrial sponsors, and resource organizations across domains including environmental effects analysis, resource management, ecological research into marine, freshwater, and terrestrial ecosystems, and avian hazards to aircraft. During its 1991, 1992, and 1993 taxation years, LGL executed four distinct SR&ED projects examining the environmental effects of offshore oil and gas development on whales, birds, and fish.

The operational architecture of all four projects was anchored in Canada. LGL's Canadian scientific personnel conceived the research initiatives, formulated the underlying scientific hypotheses, designed the observational and experimental protocols, assimilated and analyzed the resulting datasets, tested the hypotheses against empirical findings, formulated scientific conclusions, and authored the final technical reports at LGL's Canadian facilities. However, because the offshore oil and gas extraction and transportation activities under investigation were occurring in coastal Alaska, the physical observation of the target marine and avian species—and the raw collection of behavioural and ecological field data—had to be executed on location in parts of coastal Alaska where oil and gas had been extracted and transported. Following field acquisition, the raw data was transported back to LGL's Canadian premises for scientific processing and synthesis.

In filing its corporate income tax returns for the 1991, 1992, and 1993 taxation years, LGL claimed that the four initiatives constituted unified Canadian SR&ED projects. Consequently, the taxpayer included the direct costs of the Alaskan field data collection, together with the portion of corporate overhead expenditures allocable to those Alaskan field operations, as current expenditures "on scientific research and experimental development carried on in Canada" pursuant to subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Act, claiming corresponding refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credits pursuant to subsections 127(5) and 127(9).
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister of National Revenue (administered by Revenue Canada, now the Canada Revenue Agency or "CRA") reassessed LGL for the 1991, 1992, and 1993 taxation years. Notably, the Minister did not dispute that the four projects, when evaluated as scientific endeavours, satisfied the technical definition of SR&ED under Regulation 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations (the "Regulations"). Nor did the Minister challenge the eligibility of the salaries, wages, and overhead incurred for the hypothesis formulation, data analysis, and report preparation physically performed at LGL's offices in Canada.

Instead, the Crown challenged the territorial nexus of the Alaskan field expenditures. The Minister disallowed subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) pooling and subsections 127(5) and 127(9) refundable ITCs in respect of all direct data collection costs and allocable overhead incurred in Alaska. The tax authority maintained that because the physical acts of observation and data gathering took place outside Canada's territorial boundaries, those specific expenditures were incurred in respect of SR&ED carried on outside Canada. As a result, the Crown reclassified the Alaskan costs under subsection 37(2) of the Act, which permitted a current income deduction for foreign research expenditures directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, but excluded them from the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and barred them from generating refundable or non-refundable ITCs.
Governing Statutory Framework

During the 1991–1993 taxation years at issue (under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, as amended, and carried forward into R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), the statutory regime governing SR&ED incentives operated through the interplay of three primary legislative mechanisms. First, with respect to the substantive definition of SR&ED, subsection 37(7) referred to Regulation 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations (subsequently consolidated into subsection 248(1) of the Act) to define "scientific research and experimental development" as systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis—encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development—and explicitly including directly commensurate support work such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research.

Second, with respect to the domestic SR&ED expenditure pool and overhead rules, subsection 37(1) authorized a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct in computing business income the aggregate of amounts, "each of which is an expenditure of a current nature made by the taxpayer in the year... (i) on scientific research and experimental development carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer". Under the rules now found in subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Act and paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations (which govern what has been called the traditional method since the elective proxy method was introduced after the taxation years at issue), eligible expenditures include overhead and other expenditures directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Third, regarding the dichotomy between foreign SR&ED deductions and Investment Tax Credit eligibility, subsection 37(2) provided a separate, standalone current-year deduction for expenditures of a current nature made on SR&ED "carried on outside Canada", directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer and related to the taxpayer's business. Crucially, the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) for the purpose of earning SR&ED Investment Tax Credits under subsection 127(5) incorporated expenditures described in subsection 37(1), while omitting expenditures governed by subsection 37(2).
The Court's Final Holding

The Tax Court of Canada dismissed LGL's appeal from the assessments, and the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed LGL's further appeal with costs. Writing for a unanimous panel of the Federal Court of Appeal (McDonald J.A., with Robertson and Rothstein JJ.A. concurring), the Court affirmed Judge Bowman's conclusion that subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) operates on a strict, granular expenditure-by-expenditure basis rather than on a monolithic project basis. Even where foreign data collection cannot physically be performed inside Canada, does not constitute standalone SR&ED in isolation, and forms an indispensable component of a research project conceived, managed, and analyzed in Canada by Canadian scientists, the direct costs and allocable overhead of the activities physically executed outside Canada are not expenditures on SR&ED "carried on in Canada". Such costs fall exclusively under subsection 37(2) and are statutorily disqualified from generating SR&ED Investment Tax Credits.

Federal Court of Appeal: McDonald J.A. (writing), Robertson and Rothstein JJ.A. (concurring), February 7, 2000. Tax Court of Canada: Bowman T.C.J., January 12, 1999.
Taxation Years at Issue
1991, 1992, and 1993 corporate taxation years.
Core Technical Projects
Four environmental SR&ED projects investigating the environmental effects of offshore oil and gas development on whales, birds, and fish.
Disputed Expenditures
Direct field data collection costs and allocable corporate overhead incurred in coastal Alaska, claimed for refundable ITCs under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and subsections 127(5) and 127(9).
Key Statutory Provisions
Income Tax Act (Canada), s. 37(1)(a)(i), s. 37(2), s. 37(8), s. 127(5), s. 127(9) (and modern s. 248(1), s. 37(1.3), s. 37(1.4)/(1.5)); Income Tax Regulations, Reg. 2900(1), Reg. 2900(2)(c).
Appellate Disposition

Appeal dismissed with costs; the Court expressly disagreed with the Tax Court decisions in Tigney Technology Inc. v. R. (97 D.T.C. 414) and Data Kinetics Ltd. v. R. (98 D.T.C. 1877), and reversed Tigney Technology in the companion appeal heard in tandem.

body.text: 2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of LGL's Alaskan expenditures did not stem from a classic scientific failure to prove technological uncertainty, technological advancement, or systematic investigation. On the contrary, the Crown and the Courts accepted that the four projects satisfied the scientific criteria of Regulation 2900. Rather, the taxpayer's defeat resulted from a fundamental legal, structural, and accounting failure: LGL structured its operations and tax filing around the erroneous legal premise that the domestic centre of gravity of a research project legally absorbs and domesticates physical support activities executed in foreign jurisdictions. A rigorous deconstruction of the judgments of Bowman T.C.J. and McDonald J.A. exposes four interconnected legal and evidentiary failures that dictated the outcome.
Failure to Separate Project-Level Qualification from Expenditure-Level Territoriality

The central legal flaw in LGL's litigation strategy was its conflation of the threshold definition of an SR&ED project under Regulation 2900 with the expenditure deductibility and credit mechanics of subsection 37(1). At trial before Judge Bowman, LGL successfully established four critical findings of fact, recorded at paragraph 44 of the Tax Court judgment. First, LGL demonstrated geographic necessity, proving that the observation of marine mammals, birds, and fish in areas where oil and gas had been extracted and transported had to be conducted in coastal Alaska and could not physically have been performed inside Canada. Second, LGL established the dependent SR&ED status of the field work, showing that viewed in complete isolation, the raw field observation and data gathering in Alaska did not constitute standalone SR&ED, but rather acquired the character of SR&ED only because those activities were assimilated into and made an integral part of the broader scientific projects conducted in Canada. Third, the taxpayer proved scientific indispensability, confirming that the assembly of the Alaskan field data was an essential and necessary prerequisite to the execution of the overall Canadian research projects. Fourth, LGL established the predominant Canadian character of the initiatives, convincing Judge Bowman that if it were relevant to designate each project, looked at in its entirety and not piecemeal, as either "Canadian" or "non-Canadian," it would be more accurate to designate the projects as "Canadian," because the work was done by a Canadian company using Canadian researchers and personnel, and the core scientific work—the analysis of the data, the formulation and testing of hypotheses, the formation of conclusions, and the preparation of reports—was all done in Canada.

LGL argued that these four factual findings compelled a legal victory. Specifically, LGL contended that because raw data collection is a commensurate support activity that only becomes SR&ED by virtue of its integration into the core scientific analysis in Canada, severing the Alaskan data collection from the Canadian project would strip the Alaskan work of its SR&ED character altogether, violating the holistic definition of an SR&ED project under Regulation 2900.

The Federal Court of Appeal dismantled this reasoning by articulating a mandatory two-step statutory analysis. In Step 1, the tax authority and the Court examine the scientific initiative under Regulation 2900 (now subsection 248(1) of the Act) to determine whether the activities collectively constitute SR&ED. At this initial qualification stage, the project is indeed evaluated as an indivisible whole, completely irrespective of geographical borders. Thus, Alaskan field observations and Ontario laboratory analyses are aggregated to confirm that a systematic investigation by means of experiment or analysis has occurred and that the data collection is an eligible support activity.

However, once Step 1 is satisfied and the activities are stamped with the legal character of SR&ED, Regulation 2900 is exhausted, and the analysis moves to Step 2 under section 37 of the Act. At Step 2, the inquiry is no longer whether the project as a whole is SR&ED, but rather which specific pecuniary outlays qualify for the preferential domestic pool under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) versus the foreign deduction provision under subsection 37(2). Because LGL failed to recognize that SR&ED qualification (Step 1) precedes and is legally distinct from territorial expenditure allocation (Step 2), its reliance on the integrated scientific nature of the project failed to overcome the territorial bar in subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i).
Statutory Interpretation and the Collapse of the "Indivisible Whole" Doctrine

To support its contention that an SR&ED project cannot be geographically partitioned, LGL relied heavily on two prior Tax Court of Canada decisions: Tigney Technology Inc. v. R. (1997), 97 D.T.C. 414 (T.C.C.) and Data Kinetics Ltd. v. R. (1998), 98 D.T.C. 1877 (T.C.C.). In Tigney Technology and Data Kinetics, the Tax Court judges had ruled in favour of taxpayers that incurred expenditures for work performed outside Canada as part of Canadian-based R&D projects, reasoning that the wording of subsections 37(1) and 37(2) does not refer to "that portion of SR&ED" or similar language that would support the division of projects. Those earlier cases held that the activity in question should be looked at as a whole and not subdivided into its constituent parts, with Data Kinetics further reasoning that, if SR&ED projects could be subdivided, it would be uncertain whether each particular part of the project would continue to constitute SR&ED.

Hearing LGL in tandem with the appeal in Tigney Technology, the Federal Court of Appeal expressly disagreed with both Tigney Technology and Data Kinetics, and in its companion judgment reversed the Tax Court's decision in Tigney Technology. Justice McDonald grounded this conclusion in a strict textual and contextual analysis of paragraph 37(1)(a), which opens with the words: "the aggregate of all amounts each of which is an expenditure of a current nature made by the taxpayer in the year... (i) on scientific research and experimental development carried on in Canada".

The Court reasoned that, although subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) does not expressly say that SR&ED expenditures made outside Canada are to be separated out, neither does it indicate that expenditures are to be grouped by project and treated as an indivisible whole, and that the statutory phrase "each of which is an expenditure" implicitly indicates that the focus of the provision is on individual expenditures rather than on the research project as a monolithic entity. Furthermore, the Court agreed with the Tax Court Judge that the words of paragraph 37(1)(a) and subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) are clear and comprehensible, holding that where part of an SR&ED project is carried on in Canada and another part outside Canada, the only criterion is whether the expenditures were made for SR&ED activities carried on in Canada (the Crown having argued that "carried on" means to "conduct" or "engage in" in Canada). Agreeing with the Tax Court Judge, the Federal Court of Appeal held that in the face of clear wording in the Act the principles of statutory interpretation cannot be used to strain the plain meaning of the words, and it endorsed Judge Bowman's observation at paragraph 55 of the Tax Court judgment that, since a substantial part of the project was performed outside Canada, no principle of interpretation would permit the conclusion that the work forming part of the SR&ED project outside Canada was "carried on in Canada".

Beyond textual literalism, the Federal Court of Appeal identified two profound policy defects fatal to LGL's "indivisible whole" doctrine. The first defect is judicial arbitrariness and commercial uncertainty: if an entire multi-jurisdictional project had to be classified as 100% Canadian or 100% foreign, the courts would be required to determine when the parts of a project undertaken in Canada are sufficiently "integral" to justify calling the entire project "Canadian," which would inevitably lead to uncertainty for taxpayers whose SR&ED projects involve undertakings both inside and outside Canada. The second defect is the perverse disqualification of domestic R&D: an all-or-nothing project test operates as a double-edged sword. If a Canadian corporation was forced by technical necessity to conduct the majority of a project's physical testing outside Canada while conducting the remaining core research in Canadian laboratories, the holistic test would compel a court to label the entire project "non-Canadian," thereby stripping the taxpayer of SR&ED tax credits on the genuine research physically performed inside Canada. Such a result would directly contravene Parliament's legislative purpose in enacting section 37 and section 127 to provide tax incentives for research and development conducted within Canada.
Operational and Accounting Failure to Segregate Foreign Support Work and Overhead

From an evidentiary and compliance perspective, LGL's claim failed because it bundled foreign support activities and their associated overhead into its domestic ITC claim without establishing a domestic physical nexus for the execution of those tasks. In the environmental and earth sciences sector, field data collection is categorized under Regulation 2900(1)(d) (now paragraph (d) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1)) as commensurate support work. While support work inherits its scientific eligibility from the core experimental development or applied research it supports, LGL Ltd. v. R. establishes that support work does not inherit the geographic location of the core research. Each discrete support task takes its geographic situs from the physical location where the human labour, equipment operation, or observation actually occurs.

Equally significant was the disqualification of LGL's allocable corporate overhead. Under the traditional method of calculating SR&ED expenditures pursuant to the current subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Act and paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations, an overhead or other expenditure (or portion thereof) is eligible only if it satisfies a conjunctive two-prong directly attributable test: first, the expenditure must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; and second, the expenditure must be incremental, meaning it would not have been incurred had such prosecution of SR&ED in Canada not occurred.

In LGL, the taxpayer claimed the overhead allocable to the Alaskan field work, together with the direct data collection costs, as expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada and sought refundable ITCs on that overhead. Because the underlying Alaskan field data collection was legally characterized as SR&ED carried on outside Canada under subsection 37(2), any overhead incremental and directly related to those Alaskan field operations was axiomatically directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED outside Canada. As reflected in the CRA's Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (Sections 6.0 through 6.3, which cite LGL Ltd. v. The Queen and Tigney Technology Inc. v. The Queen as references), overhead and other expenditures, including foreign travel, relating to support work performed outside Canada may only be deducted as expenditures for SR&ED carried on outside Canada and are excluded from the subsection 37(1) pool, while expenditures for work outside Canada that does not itself constitute SR&ED can qualify only in limited cases, such as acquiring equipment or materials for SR&ED in Canada, training hands-on employees, or visiting foreign customers about SR&ED carried on in Canada. The Federal Court of Appeal noted at paragraph 21 of its judgment that the Tax Court Judge foresaw little difficulty in reasonably dividing LGL's costs between activities inside and outside Canada, and agreed that this was a more reasonable result than deciding whether a project carried on both inside and outside Canada is essentially "Canadian" or essentially "non-Canadian," thereby underscoring cost segregation as a practical necessity for Canadian claimants.
Post-LGL Legislative Evolution: The Subsection 37(1.4) / 37(1.5) Carve-Out

A nuanced understanding of LGL Ltd. v. R. requires examining its direct legislative aftermath. During the 1991–1993 taxation years litigated in LGL, the Income Tax Act contained no statutory relief whatsoever for salaries paid to Canadian-resident employees travelling abroad to perform integral SR&ED support work. Some years after LGL and Tigney Technology, in response to the position of Canadian R&D enterprises that faced unavoidable foreign testing requirements (such as climatic, seismic, marine, or regulatory testing unavailable in Canada), Parliament enacted a targeted statutory exception through the Budget Implementation Act, 2008: subsection 37(1.4) (Salary or wages for SR&ED outside Canada) and subsection 37(1.5) (Salary or wages outside Canada — limit determined), which apply to expenditures made after February 25, 2008 and are referenced in CRA administrative policy.

Under this modern statutory carve-out, a limited portion of "permissible salary or wages" paid to an employee for SR&ED work physically performed outside Canada is deemed, for the purposes of section 37, section 127, and Part XXIX of the Regulations, to be an expenditure made in respect of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer, provided strict statutory conditions are satisfied. Specifically, the employee performing the foreign SR&ED work must be a resident of Canada at the time the expense is incurred, and the foreign SR&ED work must be directly undertaken by the taxpayer, related to a business of the taxpayer, and solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer; in addition, under paragraph 37(9)(b), the taxpayer must reasonably believe that the salary or wages are not subject to an income or profits tax imposed by the foreign country because of the employee's presence or activity there. Furthermore, the maximum amount of foreign salaries deemed to be incurred in Canada cannot exceed 10% of the total salary or wages paid in the taxation year to employees in respect of SR&ED carried on in Canada and directly undertaken by the taxpayer. Payments to foreign subcontractors, foreign third-party service providers, foreign vessel or facility charters, and foreign travel outlays remain completely outside this carve-out. Consequently, while the core legal doctrine of LGL Ltd. v. R. remains the governing law of Canada—barring all foreign third-party contracts, foreign materials, foreign equipment leases, foreign travel expenses, and any foreign employee salaries exceeding the 10% domestic wage cap—modern SR&ED tax advisors must synthesize the judicial rule in LGL with the narrow statutory safe harbour for Canadian-resident employee wages.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and legal requirement examined in LGL Ltd. v. R. against the taxpayer's legal and evidentiary position and the authoritative standard of proof established by the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal.

headers: Taxpayer's Position & Evidentiary Approach in LGL Ltd. v. R.
Court's Standard of Proof & Authoritative Legal Holding

cells: Regulation 2900(1) (Now ITA s. 248(1)): Threshold Qualification of an SR&ED Project and Commensurate Support Work (Data Collection)

LGL argued that because the Alaskan field data collection was not SR&ED on its own and only became SR&ED when assimilated into the Canadian hypothesis-testing project, the project had to be treated as an indivisible whole for all purposes under the Act.

Two-Step Analytical Separation: At Step 1 (Regulation 2900 / s. 248(1)), the Court evaluates the project as an indivisible whole without regard to geographic borders to determine whether systematic investigation and eligible support work exist. Qualifying at Step 1 does not confer domestic territorial status at Step 2.
ITA Paragraph 37(1)(a): Granular Expenditure Focus ("each of which is an expenditure of a current nature")

LGL relied on Tigney Technology and Data Kinetics to argue that section 37 lacks partitioning words ("that portion of SR&ED") and therefore requires classifying the entire project holistically as either 100% Canadian or 100% non-Canadian.

Expenditure-by-Expenditure Test: The phrase "each of which is an expenditure" indicates that territorial eligibility is assessed at the level of each individual expenditure, not at the monolithic project level. The Court expressly disagreed with Tigney Technology and Data Kinetics, reversing Tigney Technology in the companion appeal heard in tandem.
ITA Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i): Territorial Nexus ("on scientific research and experimental development carried on in Canada")

LGL proved that the projects were conceived, managed, analyzed, and reported in Canada by Canadian scientists, and that collecting data in Alaska was physically unavoidable because the oil and gas impacts occurred there.

Strict Physical Situs Standard: "Carried on in Canada" bears its plain, unambiguous territorial meaning. Physical necessity and domestic intellectual direction cannot legally transform activities physically executed outside Canada into work "carried on in Canada".
ITA Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) & Regulation 2900(2)(c): Directly Related and Incremental Overhead Expenditures
LGL pooled corporate overhead allocable to the Alaskan data collection into its domestic SR&ED claim on the basis that the overhead supported an overarching Canadian SR&ED project.

Derivative Territorial Disqualification: The Court held that the direct costs and the allocable overhead for the work done outside Canada do not come within subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and therefore do not give rise to the refundable ITC. Under the current traditional-method rules, overhead must be directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada to qualify under Reg. 2900(2)(c), so overhead allocable to foreign field support work is attributable to foreign SR&ED and excluded from s. 37(1) and ITCs.
ITA Subsection 37(2) vs. Subsections 127(5) & 127(9): Segregation of Foreign SR&ED Costs from Qualified Expenditures for ITCs

LGL did not segregate Alaskan field collection costs and associated overhead into subsection 37(2), claiming refundable ITCs under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) on the unified project expenditure total.

Cost Partitioning: Where part of an SR&ED project is carried on in Canada and another part outside Canada, the only criterion is whether each expenditure was made for SR&ED activities carried on in Canada; the Court agreed with the Tax Court Judge that the costs could reasonably be divided between domestic activities (eligible for s. 37(1) pooling and s. 127(5)/(9) ITCs) and foreign activities (restricted to current deduction under s. 37(2), which does not give rise to the refundable ITC).

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the appellate jurisprudence of LGL Ltd. v. R. and the subsequent statutory architecture of the Income Tax Act (Canada) into actionable tax and operational strategy, the following two industry case studies examine Canadian corporations confronting the exact territorial pitfalls that defeated LGL Limited. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step remedial blueprint across project governance, technical documentation, contract structuring, and financial tracking.
Case Study 1: Offshore Marine Acoustics & Autonomous Sensor Array Engineering (Ocean Technology Sector)
Operational Scenario and LGL Vulnerability Exposure

Pelagic Sonar Dynamics Inc. ("Pelagic"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) headquartered in Halifax, Nova Scotia, is developing a novel real-time hydrophone signal-processing algorithm and autonomous subsurface mooring array designed to detect and differentiate low-frequency baleen whale vocalizations amidst high-decibel subsea seismic airgun impulses and commercial shipping cavitation noise. The core technological uncertainty involves overcoming severe multipath acoustic reverberation and Doppler distortion in shallow-shelf marine thermal layers where existing fast-Fourier transform (FFT) and wavelet denoising models fail.

To train and validate the acoustic attenuation hypotheses, Pelagic's engineers need acoustic propagation datasets captured during active offshore industrial seismic surveying in sub-Arctic shallow-shelf bathymetry inhabited by migrating bowhead whales. Because regulatory moratoria currently restrict active commercial airgun arrays in comparable Canadian waters during the target migration window, Pelagic plans to charter a research vessel in the Beaufort Sea off Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, for a six-week marine field campaign. Under its initial project plan, Pelagic intends to send four Nova Scotia acoustic engineers to Alaska for six weeks, subcontract a local Alaskan marine survey firm to deploy and recover the hydrophone moorings, and claim 100% of the vessel charter, Alaskan subcontractor fees, travel expenses, engineer salaries, and allocable Halifax corporate overhead as part of a single "Canadian SR&ED project" under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and subsection 127(5).

Under the direct precedent of LGL Ltd. v. R., Pelagic's initial structure is fatally flawed. While the overall acoustic initiative qualifies as SR&ED at Step 1 under subsection 248(1), the CRA will invoke Step 2 of LGL to disallow subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) treatment and refundable CCPC Investment Tax Credits on the Alaskan subcontractor fees, the foreign vessel charter, the travel costs, the allocable corporate overhead, and any foreign-incurred salaries exceeding statutory limits, relegating those outlays to non-creditable deductions under subsection 37(2).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance and Domestic Activity Repatriation

Pelagic must restructure its engineering governance to sever passive foreign data acquisition from active experimental development, shifting the maximum possible volume of physical experimentation into Canadian territory and Canadian waters. Before any foreign deployment, Pelagic's governance committee must mandate that controlled multi-path acoustic calibration and synthetic airgun impulse testing be executed inside Canada—specifically at an indoor anechoic hydro-acoustic test tank in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, followed by open-water trials within the Emerald Basin of the Scotian Shelf, which lies within Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone, where expenditures made in the course of a business carried on in Canada for the prosecution of SR&ED are deemed to be made "in Canada" pursuant to subsection 37(1.3) of the Act. By using calibrated underwater acoustic transducers in Canadian waters to replicate the acoustic impedance of industrial seismic arrays, Pelagic converts what would have been six weeks of Alaskan experimentation into five weeks of domestic Canadian experimentation under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and subsection 37(1.3). Furthermore, for the irreducible empirical baseline data that can only be captured during active Alaskan seismic operations, Pelagic must eliminate the six-week on-site deployment of four Canadian engineers. Instead, governance protocols must restrict the Alaskan activity to a brief physical deployment of autonomous, satellite-linked acoustic buoys by a single Halifax staff technician. Once moored in Alaskan waters, the buoys transmit raw acoustic packets via satellite uplink directly to Pelagic's Halifax laboratory server, ensuring that all real-time adaptive filtering adjustments, parameter tuning, and hypothesis testing are executed physically at workstations in Halifax by Canadian engineers analyzing the live telemetry stream.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous T661 Structuring

On Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), Pelagic must avoid describing the Alaskan buoy deployment as an undifferentiated phase of the experimental development. Pelagic's technical narratives in Part 2 of Form T661 must explicitly reflect the two-step distinction in LGL by anchoring the technological uncertainties, hypotheses, and systematic analytical iterations within the Halifax laboratory and the Scotian Shelf (Canadian EEZ) marine trials. To prove under the LGL expenditure-by-expenditure standard that the adaptive algorithm modifications occurred "in Canada", Pelagic must maintain contemporaneous Git commit logs, simulation execution logs, and satellite command uplink records bearing Halifax IP addresses alongside employee physical access logs at the Nova Scotia facility. This evidentiary record establishes that while raw acoustic waves entered a hydrophone in Alaska, the human systematic investigation and experimental manipulation occurred physically in Nova Scotia.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring and Subsection 37(1.4) / 37(1.5) Wage Optimization

Pelagic must overhaul its third-party contracts and employee deployment schedules to prevent subsection 37(2) disallowances. Under LGL and subsections 37(1.4)/(1.5), payments to foreign subcontractors for SR&ED carried on outside Canada are 100% excluded from ITCs. Pelagic must therefore cancel the turnkey Alaskan marine survey subcontract and instead contract all sensor array fabrication, pressure-housing design, and firmware programming to Canadian engineering firms in Nova Scotia, qualifying those outlays as domestic SR&ED contracts under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), subject to the rule that only 80% of arm's-length contract payments count as qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. The Alaskan vessel charter must be contracted strictly as a commercial logistical drop-off service isolated from the SR&ED claim, minimizing its cost footprint. Simultaneously, for the single Canadian-resident technician who travels to Alaska for ten days total to calibrate, deploy, and recover the autonomous moorings, Pelagic should invoke subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5). Because the technician is a Canadian resident directly employed by Pelagic, and the ten days of Alaskan calibration are directly undertaken by Pelagic and solely in support of the Halifax SR&ED project, 100% of that technician's salary for the ten days in Alaska is deemed to be an expenditure on SR&ED "carried on in Canada", provided those wages remain beneath 10% of Pelagic's total domestic SR&ED payroll for the taxation year.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Overhead Allocation Remediation

To prevent the overhead disqualification suffered by LGL Limited, whose overhead allocable to the work done outside Canada was held not to come within subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), Pelagic must restructure its overhead accounting methodology. Rather than using the Traditional Method—which requires claimants to prove under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c) that overhead costs are directly related and incremental to SR&ED in Canada, and under which overhead tied to Alaskan activities would be excluded consistent with LGL—Pelagic should elect the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act. Under the PPA method, Pelagic calculates its notional overhead for ITC purposes as a statutory percentage of the directly engaged SR&ED salary base. Furthermore, Section 6.3 of the CRA's Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy states that, under the traditional method, no overhead and other expenditures can be allowed under subsection 37(1) in relation to permissible salary or wages for SR&ED performed outside Canada that are deemed under subsections 37(1.4)/(1.5) (within the 10% cap) to be incurred for SR&ED in Canada; accordingly, actual foreign travel and lodging costs must be tracked in a segregated general ledger cost centre and claimed solely as a current deduction under subsection 37(2) without contaminating the Form T661 ITC calculation.
Case Study 2: Sub-Tropical Agronomic Biostimulant & Pathogen Resistance Development (Agricultural Biotechnology Sector)
Operational Scenario and LGL Vulnerability Exposure

Prairie PhytoGenomics Corp. ("PhytoGen"), an agricultural biotechnology company based in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, is conducting applied research to bioengineer a synthetic endophytic bacterial consortium capable of inducing systemic resistance in leguminous crops against a virulent soil-borne fungal pathogen (Fusarium wilt variant) under high-heat, high-salinity soil stress. PhytoGen's molecular biologists in Saskatoon sequence the microbial transcriptomes, perform CRISPR-Cas9 metabolic pathway edits, and formulate the liquid inoculant prototypes.

To achieve two full generational crop cycles within a single 12-month taxation year and test the microbial consortium under naturally occurring high-salinity, high-temperature soil conditions during the Canadian winter (November through March), PhytoGen leases an agricultural test plot in Sinaloa, Mexico, and contracts a Mexican agronomy institute to plant treated seed cohorts, apply pathogen stressors, record plant phenotyping data, and harvest root tissue samples. The root tissue and raw phenotypic logs are shipped back to Saskatoon in April for metagenomic sequencing and statistical variance analysis. PhytoGen claims all costs of the Mexican winter field trials—including plot lease fees, Mexican agronomy institute contract payments, Saskatoon scientists' winter travel to Mexico, and allocated Saskatoon laboratory overhead—as Canadian SR&ED under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), asserting that the Mexican winter growth cycle is merely a biological "data collection" step essential to a Canadian genomics project.

Under LGL Ltd. v. R., the CRA will audit and deny ITCs on the entire Mexican winter trial operation. Even if the Tax Court were to agree with PhytoGen (as Judge Bowman agreed with LGL at paragraph 44) that growing crops in outdoor high-temperature winter soil had to be done outside Canada during November through March, that the field cultivation was not SR&ED on its own, and that the resulting root data was essential to the Saskatoon genomics project, the expenditure-by-expenditure rule of LGL dictates that every dollar expended on physical cultivation, observation, and data collection in Mexico is an expenditure on SR&ED carried on outside Canada under subsection 37(2).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Project Governance and Domestic Environmental Simulation

PhytoGen must challenge the false assumption of geographic necessity by replacing outdoor foreign winter field trials with controlled-environment domestic experimentation. In LGL, the Tax Court found as a fact that the data collection had to be done outside Canada and could not have been done in Canada, because the target species were observed in parts of coastal Alaska where oil and gas had been extracted and transported. In contrast, agricultural soil salinity, thermal stress, photoperiods, and fungal pathogen inoculation can be replicated inside Canada during winter. PhytoGen's project governance must redirect the winter trial budget toward leasing high-capacity controlled-environment phytotron growth chambers at the University of Saskatchewan or National Research Council facilities in Saskatoon. If specific Mexican or sub-tropical saline soil chemistry or pathogen strains are required to test the hypothesis, PhytoGen should obtain federal containment permits to import sterilized or quarantined soil samples and fungal isolates into its containment greenhouse in Saskatoon. Under the LGL expenditure-by-expenditure physical situs test, purchasing and shipping a physical sample to Canada to perform the biological growth, stress induction, and phenotypic data collection inside a Saskatoon phytotron renders 100% of the cultivation, observation, and analysis "scientific research and experimental development carried on in Canada" under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i).
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Experimentation Records

To insulate the repatriated winter experiments and any residual foreign commercial validation from CRA recharacterization, PhytoGen must rigorously separate its technical documentation. If PhytoGen still conducts a small-scale outdoor plot trial in Mexico for commercial regulatory registration or customer demonstration, project governance records must formally sever that commercial trial from the Form T661 SR&ED project definition. The Form T661 project description must define the scientific advancement and hypothesis testing exclusively around the controlled multi-variable experimental matrices executed in the Saskatoon phytotrons, where temperature, humidity, soil electrical conductivity (EC), and pathogen load are systematically varied and measured inside Canada. Contemporaneous electronic laboratory notebooks must log daily phenotypic measurements, chlorophyll fluorescence readings, and root exudate sampling with explicit physical room numbers in the Saskatoon facility, eliminating any evidentiary ambiguity regarding where the support data collection occurred.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring and Domestic Institutional Subcontracting

PhytoGen must restructure its external research agreements to comply with the domestic territoriality rules of paragraph 37(1)(a). Instead of paying the Mexican agronomy institute—which fails subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i) and (i.01) under LGL because the work is performed outside Canada and fails subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii) because it is neither carried on in Canada nor paid to an approved Canadian university, association, or research institute—PhytoGen should execute a collaborative research agreement or fee-for-service SR&ED contract with a Canadian university faculty of agriculture or a Canadian contract research organization resident in Canada to execute the winter phytotron stress trials inside Canada. Payments to a Canadian corporation or approved Canadian institution for SR&ED physically carried on in Canada qualify for section 37(1) pooling and for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits, subject to the rule that only 80% of arm's-length contract payments count as qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. Furthermore, if a Canadian-resident PhD agronomist employed by PhytoGen must travel to Mexico for four days solely to collect wild native endophyte strains from arid soils to bring back to Saskatoon for genomic sequencing, PhytoGen must ensure no Mexican contractor is paid to perform research. The Canadian scientist's four-day salary is claimed under the subsections 37(1.4)/(1.5) 10% permissible wage rule as work solely in support of the Saskatoon project, while airfare and hotel outlays are isolated in non-creditable accounts.
Step 4: Financial Tracking and Granular Cost-Centre Accounting

To satisfy Judge Bowman's mandate that costs be reasonably divided between domestic and foreign activities, PhytoGen must implement granular cost-centre accounting. PhytoGen must configure its enterprise resource planning (ERP) and time-tracking system so that every employee timesheet entry and vendor invoice requires both an SR&ED Project Task Code and a mandatory Physical Location Tag distinguishing Saskatchewan operations from foreign travel. Because PhytoGen operates a capital-intensive wet laboratory and phytotron facility in Saskatoon with high incremental utilities, specialized gases, and facility costs, it may use the Traditional Method under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and paragraph 2900(2)(c) rather than electing the Proxy Method. By shifting the winter growth trials from outdoor plots in Mexico into the Saskatoon phytotron facility, 100% of the incremental electricity, environmental chamber maintenance, and consumable reagents incurred during the winter cycle satisfy the two-prong test of paragraph 2900(2)(c)—being both directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—thereby converting previously disqualified foreign overhead into fully creditable Canadian SR&ED expenditures.
